issues.legal_issue: A writ petition seeking to invalidate registered property documents may be declined where the petitioner has already pursued an efficacious alternative remedy for the same dispute, particularly when the petition would require resolution of disputed facts and the petitioner has pursued multiple proceedings.
material_facts: The appellant had already filed a cooperative dispute challenging the society’s cancellation of the original allotment and the subsequent allotment to another person; that dispute remained pending.
The appellant separately asked registration officials to cancel the same registered documents and initiated other proceedings concerning them.
The appellant had entered into a compromise concerning the property and accepted consideration, but did not refund it after being asked to do so.
The writ petition sought substantially the same relief as the pending cooperative dispute, including declarations invalidating the registered documents.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in dismissing the writ petition. The appellant remained free to pursue the statutory remedy already invoked or another remedy available in law, and the issues were to be decided there on their merits.
issues.legal_principle: Relief under Article 226 of the Constitution is extraordinary, discretionary, and equitable. A court may decline to exercise that jurisdiction where an efficacious alternative remedy is already being pursued for the same cause, multiple proceedings have been brought, or disputed facts require adjudication elsewhere. A writ is not ordinarily a means to declare private rights or enforce contractual rights. The society’s decision to cancel an allotment or membership concerns its business and may be challenged before the competent cooperative forum under Section 64 of the Madhya Pradesh Cooperative Societies Act, 1960. The court relied on the established principles governing discretionary writ relief and distinguished the circumstances discussed in Pratap Singh v. State of Punjab.

predicates.is_writ_challenging_private_property_doc: The petitioner brought a writ proceeding seeking relief against documents or decisions concerning private property rights.
predicates.alternative_efficacious_remedy_pending: The petitioner had already invoked an available and effective remedy before a competent forum, and that proceeding remained pending.
predicates.same_relief_pursued_in_multiple_proceedi: The petitioner sought substantially the same relief through more than one proceeding.
predicates.disputed_facts_require_adjudication: Resolving the claim required a forum to determine contested facts or assess evidence.

issues.definition: When a property-related writ duplicates relief sought in a pending effective proceeding, involves disputed facts, and forms part of multiple proceedings, the writ court may decline relief while leaving another remedy open.

issues.legal_issue: Registration officials have no authority to cancel the registration of a document after it has been registered when no law confers that power on them.
material_facts: After the documents had been registered, the appellant applied to the Sub-Registrar to cancel their registration; the Sub-Registrar rejected the application, stating that the registration process had concluded and that he lacked cancellation jurisdiction.
The appellant then applied to the Inspector General of Registration, who rejected the request on the ground that his powers were limited to general superintendence and rule-making.
The appellant sought cancellation of the registrations through the registration authorities rather than only challenging the documents before a competent court or forum.
issues.conclusion: Neither the Sub-Registrar nor the Inspector General of Registration had authority to cancel the registration of documents that had already been registered.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Registration Act, 1908, the registering officer’s role is discharged once registration is completed. The Act contains no express power for the Registrar or Sub-Registrar to recall or cancel a completed registration; the Inspector General’s supervisory and rule-making powers do not include such a power. The appeal procedure under Section 72 concerns refusal to register, not cancellation of a completed registration. The Court relied on Section 17, the provisions governing presentation and registration, Sections 68, 69 and 72, and Government of U.P. v. Raja Mohammad Amir Ahmad Khan.

predicates.is_request_to_registration_officials_to_: A person asked a registration official to cancel the registration of a document after the official had registered it.
predicates.no_law_confers_cancellation_power: No applicable law gives the registration official authority to cancel a completed registration.

issues.definition: If a person seeks cancellation of a completed registration and no law gives the registration official that power, the official cannot cancel it.

issues.legal_issue: In the absence of an applicable rule requiring the other party’s participation, unilateral presentation of an extinguishment document by a housing society does not, by itself, make its registration invalid.
material_facts: A housing society presented an extinguishment deed for registration to record its decision to cancel a member’s plot allotment after an alleged failure to build on the plot.
The original allottee or her representative was not present when the society presented the deed.
The deed was registered, and no applicable Madhya Pradesh provision or rule requiring both parties’ signatures or presence was identified.
The deed concerned the society’s decision about an allotment and membership, rather than cancellation of a sale deed between private parties.
issues.conclusion: The unilateral presentation and registration of the extinguishment deed could not be treated as fraudulent or void solely because the other party was not present. The rule in Thota Ganga Laxmi did not apply generally because it concerned an express Andhra Pradesh rule; the validity of the society’s underlying cancellation decision remained for the competent forum to decide.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 32, 34 and 35 of the Registration Act, 1908 do not require both parties to be present when a document is presented for registration, and the registering officer’s inquiry is not a quasi-judicial determination of title or the document’s substantive legality. A procedural irregularity does not by itself establish fraud or nullity; Section 87 protects acts done in good faith from invalidity merely for procedural defects. A registered document may be challenged before a competent court. Thota Ganga Laxmi v. Government of Andhra Pradesh applied an express requirement in Rule 26(k)(i) of the Andhra Pradesh Registration Rules and did not establish a universal rule. The Court also relied on Yanala Malleshwari v. Ananthula Sayamma and Park View Enterprises v. State of Tamil Nadu.

predicates.is_unilateral_extinguishment_document_pr: A party presented an extinguishment or cancellation document for registration without the other party joining in its presentation.
predicates.no_applicable_rule_requires_both_parties: No applicable law or rule requires the other party to sign the document or be present for its registration.
predicates.registration_requirements_are_followed: The document was presented and processed in accordance with the applicable registration procedure.

issues.definition: When an extinguishment document is presented by one party, no applicable rule requires both parties, and the registration procedure is followed, unilateral presentation alone does not invalidate registration.
